summary: Defines an SMIng language extension mapping SMIng definitions of identities, classes, attributes and events to SNMP nodes, scalars, tables and notifications. This is how SMIng would be used with the SNMP framework. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: This translates the new way of describing device info into the older form the common monitoring tool already understands.

questions: how to map smiing to snmp mib
subtitle: Translating next-generation device descriptions for the SNMP management framework

tldr.problem: SMIng (Structure of Management Information, Next Generation) is a modern protocol-independent language for defining network device information, but network management tools rely on SNMP, an older protocol with its own way of representing managed objects.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a language extension that maps SMIng definitions of identities, classes, attributes, and events into SNMP nodes, scalars, tables, and notifications, along with the data type conversions needed to bridge the two systems.
tldr.outcome: Device vendors can write management definitions once in SMIng and automatically generate SNMP-compatible MIBs, allowing new definitions to work with existing monitoring infrastructure without manual translation.

today: RFC 3781 is an Experimental specification providing the formal framework for mapping SMIng definitions to SNMP. It has not been obsoleted and serves as the specification for SMIng-to-SNMP translation in network management tool implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SMIng (Structure of Management Information, Next Generation) is defined in RFC 3780 as a protocol-independent data definition language. It is more flexible and expressive than earlier management information languages. However, the Internet's network management infrastructure is built around SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol), which uses a specific representation of managed objects in Management Information Bases (MIBs).

This RFC defines a set of language extensions for SMIng that allow definitions written in SMIng to be mapped to SNMP-compliant managed objects. The mapping covers how SMIng data types translate to SNMP types, and how SMIng classes, identities, attributes, and events map to SNMP nodes, scalars, tables, and notifications. The result is that a single SMIng module can be compiled into an SNMP MIB that works with existing network management tools and frameworks.
sections.plainLanguage: SMIng is the new way to describe a device. SNMP is the old way. This tells you how to say the same thing in both languages.

sections.title: SNMP Management Framework Basics
sections.content:
SNMP organizes managed objects hierarchically in an object identifier tree, where each node has a unique numeric identifier. Nodes can represent simple grouping points, scalars (single-valued objects), tables (rows of columnar objects), notifications (unsolicited messages), or compliance definitions. Scalar objects have exactly one instance, identified by appending a single 0 sub-identifier. Table row objects are distinguished using index values that make each row unique.

The RFC defines how SMIng constructs map to these SNMP node types. An SMIng identity maps to a node. Simple class attributes map to scalars, while more complex attributes or classes map to table structures with rows and columnar objects. SMIng event definitions become notifications in SNMP. The mapping also covers group definitions (which bundle objects for compliance purposes) and compliance statements (which specify implementation requirements).
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP has a filing cabinet with numbered drawers. This explains how to put your new-style description into those numbered drawers.

sections.title: Data Type Mappings
sections.content:
SMIng supports base types including OctetString, Integer32, Integer64, Unsigned32, Unsigned64, Float32, Float64, Enumeration, Bits, and ObjectIdentifier. SNMP supports a more limited set: INTEGER, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER, IpAddress, Counter32, Counter64, TimeTicks, Opaque, and Unsigned32.

The mapping converts SMIng types to SNMP equivalents. Most map directly (e.g., OctetString to OCTET STRING). Floating-point types (Float32, Float64, Float128) and 64-bit integer types are wrapped in the Opaque type with ASN.1 encoding, since SNMP does not natively support them. For example, Integer64 is BER-encoded and placed in an Opaque container. This allows SMIng's richer type system to be represented in SNMP while maintaining backward compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: SMIng can describe fancy number types (like very big numbers or decimal numbers). SNMP is more limited, so the mapping wraps fancy types in a box that SNMP understands.

sections.title: Mapping Extension Statements
sections.content:
The RFC defines several extension statements for the SNMP mapping. The snmp statement is the main container for all SNMP mapping information within an SMIng module. Under it, the node statement defines nodes in the object identifier tree, the scalars statement groups scalar objects, and the table statement defines tabular structures.

Each statement has sub-clauses: an oid clause specifying the object identifier, an implements clause linking to SMIng classes or attributes, a status clause indicating whether the definition is current or historic, a description clause for documentation, and optional reference clauses. Tables support multiple indexing modes: ordinary indexes, augmentation of existing tables, sparse augmentation, and reordering of indexes, allowing SMIng structures to be flexibly mapped to SNMP table patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: The mapping language has commands like "make a group of scalars" and "make a table." Each command has options for numbering, status, and what it is for.

sections.title: Conformance and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC includes two formal SMIng modules: NMRG-SMING-SNMP-EXT defines the SNMP mapping extension statements and the standard SNMP object identifier hierarchy (internet, mgmt, experimental, private). The NMRG-SMING-SNMP module defines derived types specific to SNMP mapping, such as RowStatus, which controls row lifecycle in tables.

The mapping is designed to be both readable to humans and parseable by MIB compilers. Security considerations focus on authorization: SNMP MIBs generated from SMIng mappings should inherit the same access control semantics as the original definitions. The approach is experimental, but provides a practical bridge allowing SMIng-based device models to be deployed using SNMP management infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is defined carefully in a formal language. The mapping is experimental, but it shows how new definitions can work with old management systems.
